title.en: Civics: Election, Political Parties and Pressure Groups

text.en: Raju watched people line up outside a polling booth. "What happens after voting?" he asked.

Elections let people choose their representatives. In India every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, which is called universal adult franchise. The Election Commission conducts free and fair elections, and electronic voting machines record votes.
Political parties put forward candidates and programmes. They may be national or state parties, and the winning party or group forms the government while the others form the opposition. Coalition governments occur when no party has a majority.
Pressure groups, such as trade unions and farmers' associations, try to influence government decisions but do not contest elections.
Elections let people choose their representatives.
In India every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, which is called universal adult franchise.
The Election Commission conducts free and fair elections, and electronic voting machines record votes.
Political parties put forward candidates and programmes.
They may be national or state parties, and the winning party or group forms the government while the others form the opposition.
Coalition governments occur when no party has a majority.
Pressure groups, such as trade unions and farmers' associations, try to influence government decisions but do not contest elections.
Elections are the engine of representative democracy. In India, elections are held regularly every five years for the Lok Sabha, state legislative assemblies and local bodies.
India uses two main election methods. In direct elections, voters directly choose their MP, MLA or ward councillor by secret ballot or Electronic Voting Machine.
In indirect elections, elected representatives vote on behalf of the people—for example, the President of India and members of the Rajya Sabha are elected indirectly.
To keep elections free and fair, Article 324 of the Constitution sets up an independent Election Commission of India headed by the Chief Election Commissioner.
The Election Commission prepares updated voter rolls, allots election symbols, announces schedules, enforces the Model Code of Conduct and oversees counting.

board.text: ECI duties: rolls, symbols, code of conduct

text.en: India also introduced VVPAT—Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail—so every voter sees a printed slip confirming their EVM choice before it drops into a sealed box.
And if a voter dislikes every candidate on the ballot, India provides the NOTA option—None of the Above—to record their dissent peacefully.
Now let us look at political parties. A political party is an organised group of citizens sharing a vision who contest elections to form government and shape public policy.
World democracies follow three party systems: a single-party system like China, a two-party system like the USA and UK, and a multi-party system like India.
India's multi-party system reflects its vast linguistic, regional and social diversity. When no single party wins a majority, parties form a coalition government.
The Election Commission recognises National Parties—which have strong support across multiple states—and State or Regional Parties—which are influential within one or more states.
Regional parties in Tamil Nadu and other states voice local language, river-water and development priorities strongly in both state assemblies and Parliament.
Equally vital is the Opposition Party—the largest non-ruling party in the legislature. It questions ministers, exposes flaws in bills, and offers voters a ready alternative government.
Now let us study Pressure Groups, also called Interest Groups. Unlike political parties, pressure groups do not contest elections or aim to capture government office.

board.text: Pressure groups do NOT contest elections

text.en: Instead, pressure groups organise citizens with a shared interest—such as farmers' associations, trade unions, student federations, business chambers or environmental groups—to influence policy.

board.text: Examples: trade unions, farmer & green groups

text.en: How do pressure groups work? They submit petitions, publish research, hold peaceful rallies, meet lawmakers and raise public awareness through media.
When pressure groups operate peacefully and transparently, they give voice to workers, farmers, consumers and minorities who might otherwise be overlooked.

board.text: Positive role: giving voice to citizens

text.en: Compare a political party and a pressure group side by side: a party contests elections with a broad manifesto; a pressure group focuses on specific causes from outside government.
Public mobilisation and citizen movements—like the Chipko forest movement or Right to Information campaign—show how organised citizens can win lasting laws.
To keep elections clean, reforms target money power, fake news, criminalisation of politics and booth capturing, while encouraging every eligible youth to register at eighteen.
Voter awareness campaigns remind us never to sell a vote for cash or gifts, because a five-year government's schools, roads and hospitals depend on honest choices.
Whenever you see a news report about a public demand, ask: is this group contesting elections as a party, or persuading lawmakers as a pressure group?
Free elections, responsible parties, a constructive opposition and active pressure groups work together to keep Indian democracy responsive to every citizen.

problem.en: A state farmers' association meets the Agriculture Minister and holds a peaceful march asking for fair sugarcane prices, but does not field any election candidates. Is it a political party or a pressure group?

text.en: Check whether the group contests elections to form government.

why.en: It does not field candidates or seek ministerial office.

text.en: Check its goal and methods.

why.en: It represents one specific interest—sugarcane farmers—and persuades the government through dialogue and peaceful protest.

text.en: Classify the organisation.

why.en: It is a pressure group (interest group), not a political party.

prompt.en: A friend says Pressure groups contest elections to form the government. How will you reply?
